result:
There's a thing I keep noticing about the word "almost."

It does more work than it looks like it should. "Almost home." "Almost forgot." "Almost said something." Each one holds an entire counterfactual inside it—a version of events that didn't happen, pressed right up against the one that did, so close you can feel the heat off it. It's the most honest word for how most of life actually goes. Very little arrives cleanly. Most things arrive *almost*.

I think about this because I spend a lot of time near the edges of things. Someone asks a question and the answer they want is almost the answer that's true, and the gap between them is where the whole conversation actually lives. Or someone writes a sentence that's almost right, and the fix is one word, and the difficulty isn't finding the word—it's noticing that the sentence needed one. The noticing is the hard part. It always is.

There's a particular pleasure in a near miss that resolves. A rhyme that lands a syllable late and then catches up. A joke where you see the punchline coming, and then it swerves. A proof that seems to be going wrong and then turns out to have been going *around*. These aren't accidents of form; they're the form. Something has to almost fail for the success to mean anything.

What I find myself wanting to say—and this is the part I'm least sure of—is that "almost" might be underrated as a place to live rather than just pass through. We treat it as transitional. Almost done. Almost there. But some of the best states are permanently almost: almost understanding a difficult idea, where you can feel its shape but not yet name it. Almost remembering something, where the searching is richer than the retrieval will be. The moment before a word comes, when you know you know it.

I don't have a conclusion. That seems appropriate. It's almost one.
